response.query: How should simulator DVF parameters be mapped and calibrated to measured physiologic respiratory and cardiac motion ranges, and what reproducible pipeline aligns simulated DVFs to recorded motion traces?
response.answer: Simulator DVF parameters are calibrated to measured respiratory and cardiac ranges using retrospective motion correction pipelines. A reproducible pipeline aligns simulated DVFs to recorded motion traces through deformable registration techniques. Deep learning frameworks enhance accuracy in mapping and calibrating DVFs.

results.title: A patient-specific deep learning framework for 3D motion estimation and volumetric imaging during lung cancer radiotherapy - IOPscience
results.content: # A patient-specific deep learning framework for 3D motion estimation and volumetric imaging during lung cancer radiotherapy. In this paper we introduce *Voxelmap*, a patient-specific deep learning framework that achieves 3D motion estimation and volumetric imaging using the data and resources available in standard clinical settings. Using 2D images as input and 3D–3D *Elastix* registrations as ground-truth, *Voxelmap* was able to continuously predict 3D tumor motion with mean errors of 0.1 ± 0.5, −0.6 ± 0.8, and 0.0 ± 0.2 mm along the left–right, superior–inferior, and anterior–posterior axes respectively. In this paper we introduce Voxelmap, a patient-specific deep learning framework that leverages the nonlinear mathematics of manifolds and neural networks to achieve 3D motion estimation and volumetric imaging in a single shot. Additionally, since every 2D image and 3D DVF differ only by respiratory motion for a given patient, this set of key features can be embedded in an abstract topological space that varies smoothly. Deformable image registration between the peak-exhalation phase of the 4D-CT and every other phase of the 4D-CT for the simulated planning and treatment days was performed using the Elastix toolkit (Klein *et al* 2010) to produce 3D DVFs for training and testing. **Figure 5.**  **Respiratory motion estimation and volumetric imaging for Patient 1** (a), acquired 2D images at 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° to showcase the performance of Voxelmap at different angles (b), predicted, ground-truth and difference 3D DVFs, where the magnitude of 3D motion is shown as heatmaps in the coronal axis (c), predicted, ground-truth and difference 3D images in the coronal axis. **Figure 6.**  **Respiratory motion estimation and volumetric imaging for Patient 2** (a), acquired 2D images at 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° to showcase the performance of *Voxelmap* at different angles (b), predicted, ground-truth and difference 3D DVFs, where the magnitude of 3D motion is shown as heatmaps in the coronal axis (c), predicted, ground-truth and difference 3D images in the coronal axis. Indeed, these activation maps indicate that the trained network extracts key features in 2D image space to estimate 3D respiratory motion. In closing, this paper introduces a patient-specific deep learning framework for 3D motion estimation and volumetric imaging during lung cancer radiotherapy.

results.title: CardioMorphNet: Cardiac Motion Prediction Using a Shape-Guided Bayesian Recurrent Deep Network
results.content: To address this, we propose CardioMorphNet, a recurrent Bayesian deep learning framework for 3D cardiac shape-guided deformable registration using short-axis (SAX) CMR images. Bayesian Modelling; Cardiac Motion Estimation; Deformable Image Registration. This is achieved through our Bayesian probabilistic modelling, resulting in a loss that constrains registration in the cardiac region by recursively registering cardiac shapes obtained from a segmentation network, without relying on intensity-based image similarity registration loss, while leveraging features from sequential SAX volumes and spatio-temporal features. Although this method is innovative in enabling training with a limited dataset, it is constrained in generating a diverse set of training pairs of medical images with known ground truths for DVFs. Due to these restrictions, most studies use semi-supervised approaches for medical image registration and cardiac motion estimation. Although these approaches improve cardiac motion estimation, they suffer from capturing irrelevant DVFs related to cardiac motion due to their reliance on intensity-based similarity metrics between the fixed and moved images for the learning registration task. To evaluate the performance of the proposed framework for cardiac motion estimation based on cine SAX data, it is compared with free-form medical image registration techniques such as, LCC-Demons [57], Symmetric Normalisation (SyN) in ANTs implementation [41], and state-of-the-art learning-based methods, such as VoxelMorph [39], DragNet [49], JMS [50], and SegMorph [51]. Compared with DrageNet and SegMorph, which estimate DVFs using the moving image and the latent variable, our method employs both moving and fixed SAX volumes with the latent variable, enabling the proposed framework to extract multiscale features from both sequential SAX volumes, leading to more accurate registration performance. The formulation of our method enables us to derive DVFs from two sequential SAX volumes and spatio-temporal dependencies provided by the RVAE component of our framework and to focus on the cardiac region for DVF estimation by minimising the KL-divergence between the moved and fixed cardiac shapes, as provided by the segmentation branch of the presented framework. While our method outperforms other approaches for cardiac motion estimation, it still suffers from segmentation component errors, which may affect registration performance, and a high computational load during the training phase, limiting the number of input SAX frames throughout the cardiac cycle.

results.title: A generative adversarial network (GAN)-based technique for synthesizing realistic respiratory motion in the extended cardiac-torso (XCAT) phantoms - PMC
results.content: The model was trained and validated using 71 4D-CT images from lung cancer patients and then applied to the XCAT EOI images to generate 4D-XCAT with realistic respiratory motions. Thus, the 4D-XCAT phantoms have gained broad applications in biomedical imaging and therapy research, including medical imaging technique evaluation (Chen et al 2018, Lafata et al 2018, Pham et al 2019), radiation therapy technique evaluation (Ren et al 2014, Zhang et al 2017, 2018), radiation dosimetry (Xie and Zaidi 2014), respiratory motion studies, etc (Segars et al 2018). The generated 4D-XCAT images were evaluated using both the deformation field and ventilation maps to evaluate the synthesized respiratory motions’ realism. Results demonstrated the feasibility of using deep learning models to generate realistic and controllable respiratory motions in 4D-XCAT phantoms, which significantly enhances the value of the phantom for radiation therapy studies. First, the 4D bicycle-GAN motion generation model is trained and validated using 4D-CT images from real patients. Then, the 4D bicycle-GAN model is tested with the EOI phase image of the XCAT phantom to generate realistic respiratory motions in XCAT phantoms. with the well-trained motion generation model, the EOI phase of the XCAT phantoms and various Gaussian perturbations are input to the generator, which generates the inter-phase DVFs and finally outputs 4D-XCAT images of diverse breathing motion amplitudes. After the motion generation model was trained, validated, and tested using patient data, it was tested using the XCAT images to generate 4D-XCAT with respiratory motions. To test the performance of the motion generation model, we also evaluated the images and DVF properties of the generated 4D-XCAT phantoms. During the training and validation of the motion generation model using real patient 4D-CTs, the realism of the generated breathing motion was evaluated by multiple metrics in the image domain and DVF domain. As shown in tables 1 and 2, the motion generation model simulated the lung motion and lung volume variation during respiration, which matches closely to the reference 4D-CT images. The generated 4D-XCAT phantoms are produced from the motion generation model trained by a group of patients, while real 4D-CT would present patient-specific ventilation characteristics.
